security_spec.violation_condition: OpenSBI M-mode trap handler does not distinguish between illegal-instruction exceptions raised by `seed` CSR access from S-mode (due to SSEED=0 per spec) and other illegal-instruction exceptions, causing S-mode `seed` access attempts to be handled as generic illegal-instruction faults rather than being recognized as an access-control delegation issue that M-mode firmware should either enable (by setting SSEED/USEED) or gracefully deny with a well-defined error.
security_spec.summary: OpenSBI must explicitly configure mseccfg.SSEED/USEED after reset before handing control to S-mode; failing to set these bits leaves S/U-mode seed CSR access permanently denied, and OpenSBI's illegal-instruction trap handler must distinguish seed CSR access violations to avoid silently blocking legitimate S-mode entropy requests.

findings.finding: OpenSBI correctly sets SSEED=1 and USEED=0 in mseccfg when the Zkr extension is detected. This grants S-mode read-write access to the seed CSR while denying U-mode access. The configuration runs on all three init paths: cold boot (sbi_hart_init), warm boot, and HSM suspend-resume (sbi_hart_reinit), so SSEED is always enabled before S-mode execution.

spec_citations.excerpt: When SSEED is 0, access to the seed CSR from S-/HS-mode raises an illegal-instruction exception. When SSEED is 1, read-write access to the seed CSR from S-/HS-mode is allowed.

findings.finding: mseccfg is intentionally excluded from the HSM non-retentive suspend CSR save list. Instead of save/restore, mseccfg is reconfigured through the warm-boot path: init_warm_resume() calls sbi_hart_reinit() (sbi_init.c:490), which calls mstatus_init() (sbi_hart.c:715) to set SSEED=1/USEED=0, then sbi_hart_protection_configure() (sbi_init.c:494) sets RLB/MML. Since mseccfg is reconfigured before sbi_hart_switch_mode() returns to S-mode in sbi_hsm_hart_resume_finish() (sbi_hsm.c:484), there is no window where S-mode observes stale mseccfg state.

The M-mode illegal-instruction trap handler dispatches ALL illegal-instruction exceptions through a unified path: sbi_illegal_insn_handler() → system_opcode_insn() → sbi_emulate_csr_read(). The seed CSR (0x015) is NOT in the emulation switch table, so unrecognized CSR accesses fall through to the default SBI_ENOTSUPP return, triggering truly_illegal_insn() which redirects the trap back to S-mode with cause=CAUSE_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION. The handler cannot distinguish a seed-CSR illegal-instruction (which would occur if SSEED were 0) from any other unrecognized CSR access. Currently a potential risk because OpenSBI always sets SSEED=1 before S-mode execution; but if SSEED were ever 0 (e.g., via a future platform quirk or errata), S-mode seed access would loop with unrecoverable illegal-instruction traps rather than receiving a well-defined error.

spec_citations.excerpt: When SSEED is 0, access to the seed CSR from S-/HS-mode raises an illegal-instruction exception. When SSEED is 1, read-write access to the seed CSR from S-/HS-mode is allowed.
The Zkr extension adds the SSEED and USEED fields to the mseccfg CSR to control access to the seed CSR from U, S, or HS modes.

findings.finding: CAUSE_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION is correctly NOT delegated to S-mode via medeleg. This ensures M-mode's CSR emulation layer (which handles seed, cycle/time counters, etc.) sees the trap first. Delegating illegal-instruction to S-mode would bypass CSR emulation entirely.

The CSR emulation layer correctly omits seed CSR from its read-emulation switch table. When SSEED=1 (the normal OpenSBI configuration), S-mode accesses seed directly in hardware without trapping, so M-mode emulation is unnecessary. The emulation path only handles CSRs that M-mode must intercept (HTIMEDELTA, cycle/time counters).
